WRITTEN ANSWERS TO STARRED QUESTIONS 
Purchase of Wheat/Rice by the poor on BPL Rates 
*361. SHRI SOLIPETA RAMACHANDRA REDDY: Will the Minister   
of   CONSUMER   AFFAIRS,   FOOD   AND   PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that poor section of the people cannot buy wheat 
or rice even at 'below poverty line' rates; 
(b) if so, whether Government propose to reduce the price of wheat and 
rice for people living below poverty line; 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor; and. 
(d) whether  Government  is  going  to  start  food  for  work 
programme for the poor as an alternative; 
1 

RAJYA SABHA       [14 December, 2000] 
THE MINISTER OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHANTA KUMAR): (a) to (d> Ensuring food 
security for all, creating a hunger-free India and reforming and improving the 
Public Distribution System so as to serve the poorest of the poor in rural and 
urban areas is part of the Government's agenda. The focus of the Targetted 
Public Distribution System (TPDS) is on the families living Below Poverty 
Line (BPL). The Central Issue Price of wh eat and rice for such families is 50 
per cent, of their economic cost. A proposal to grant further relief to the 
poorest of the poor by providing them foodgrains at rates lower than the BPL 
rates is under consideration. 
Foodgrains at the rates applicable to BPL families are available for 
allotment to the State Governments for undertaking "Food for Work" 
Programmes in the States. 
World Bank's Assistance to State Governments for Agricultural Sector 
*362. SHRI GOPALSINH G. SOLANKI: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether World Bank is providing any assistance to the State 
Governments for development of agricultural sector; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the programmes being implemented with said assistance in the 
country, particularly, in Gujarat, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and Uttaranchal; 
and 
(d) the extent to which the agricultural productivity has increased in the 
State, so far? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI NITISH KUMAR): (a) 
Yes, Sir. 
(b) At the beginning of the current financial year 2000-2001, ten World 
Bank-assisted, agricultural sector related projects were under implementation. 
The project-wise details in respect of two completed and eight on-going 
World Bank assisted projects relating to different aspects of agriculture 
development, incorporating their periods, States covered, project cost, World 
Bank Loan/Credit component and cumulative disbursements since their 
inception up to 30th September, 2000 is enclosed as Statement. (See below) 
2 

[14 December, 2000]        RAJYA SABHA 
(c) Ongoing World Bank assisted agriculture sector projects currently 
in operation in different States mainly relate to soil and water conservation, 
watershed development, agriculture extension, shrimp & fish culture 
development and human resource development in agriculture sector. The 
project-wise details are given in Annexure-I. In so far as four specifically 
mentioned States are concerned, One World Bank assisted project, namely. 
Integrated Watershed Development Project—(IWDP—Hills) Phase-II is 
currently under operation in Uttaranchal Pradesh and another project, 
namely, Bihar Plateau Development Project has recently completed its 
project duration in the undivided Bihar State in June, 2000, the area covered 
by the project included the recently carved out State of Jharkhand NATP is 
currently being implemented in reconstituted Bihar and newly carved out 
State of Jharkhand both. 
(d) World Bank assisted projects, on the whole, have impact in terms 
of increase in cropping intersity and the productivity of various crops grown 
therein and augmentation of the income of the total population, from various 
agriculture based activities, such as. Crop Husbandry, Agro-forestry, Sodic 
Land Reclamation, Fish Culture, Watershed Development, Agriculture 
Extension, Dryland farming, Horticulture, Livestock development, varietal 
development of seeds and minor irrigation related facilities, infrastructural 
build up of the rural roads, marketing structure etc. Agriculture minikits, 
comprising HYV seeds or Kharif and Rabi crops and fertilizers, are under 
some of the projects given to the local farmers/beneficiaries for increasing 
agricultural productivity. Likewise, demonstration plots are also being set up 
in the project area. Minor irrigation works and water harvesting etc. also help 
in improving the agriculture productivity. It is, however, not possible to 
quantify the extent to which agricultural productivity has increased in the 
areas covered under agriculture sector based World Bank assisted Projects.

Job Opportunities 
*366. SHRI S. AGNIRAJ: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government propose to take effective measures to create the 
job opportunities for unemployed youth through setting up industries in 
Tamil Nadu; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE DEPARTMENT OF 
DISINVESTMENT, MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRIES OF 
PLANNING, STATISTICS AND PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION 
AND MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF 
ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS, AND PUBLIC GRIEVANCES OF THE 
MINISTRY OF PERSONNEL, PUBLIC GRIEVANCES AND PENSIONS 
(SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) to (c ) In the liberalised economic 
environment, private sector is playing a major role in setting up industries 
including in Tamil Nadu inter-alia for creating jobs, it is primarily the 
responsibility of the Tamil Nadu Government to develop infrastructure and 
provide a conducive environment for private sector to set up industries. 
In addition to manufacturing sector, agriculture, construction and services 
are the major sectors which create jobs. It is up to the Tamil Nadu 
Government to pursue such policies as will strengthen development of these 
sectors at the desired pace. 
The Central Government, however, plays a facilitating role in this whole 
process by way of policy intervention and taking up schemes such as growth 
centres, integrated infrastructure development centres, etc. 
The infrastructure sector such as power, roads, ports and communications 
has been opened to private sector. With this, it is expected that private sector 
investment in infrastructure will pick up momentum, including Tamil Nadu. 
For Tamil Nadu, three Growth Centres have been approved by the 
12 

[14 December, 2000]        RAJYA  SABHA 
Central Government to be located at Orgadam (District Kanchipuram), 
Triuneiveli (district Kottaboman) and Erode (District Periyar). Sums of Rs. 0.50 
crore, Rs. 9.30 crore and Rs. 10 crore respectively have been released up to March 
2000 for these Growth Centres by the Central Government. 
Five Integrated Infrastructure Development Centres have been approved for 
Tamil Nadu to be located at Madurai, Coimbatore, Chengai MGR (2) and Thiru 
Vellore. A sum of Rs. 351.63 lakh has been released up to November, 2000 for 
these centres by the Central Government. 
Production of Arecanut 
*367. SHRI H.K. JAVARE GOWDA: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) what is the total production of arecanut in the country; 
(b) the quantity contributed by Karnataka in it; 
(c) whether the total production of arecanut is sufficient to meet the 
indigenous demand; and 
(d) if so, whether we are still importing arecanut in the country and if so, 
the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI NITISH KUMAR): (a) The 
total production of arecanut in the country during 1998-99 was 330.1 thousand 
tonnes. 
(b) The quantity of arecanut produced by Karnataka during 1998- 
99 was  131.5 thousand tonnes which is about 40%  of the total 
production. 
(c) No survey has been made to assess the consumption requirement of 
arecanut however, as per rough estimates 336.2 thousand tonnes of arecanut 
was consumed during 1998-99 in the country. 
(d) During 1998-99 India imported 6707 tonnes of arecanut to meet the gap 
between production and demand.

CTBT and NPT 
*371. SHRI SURESH KALMADI: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that USA and UK want India to sign CTBT and 
NPT; 
(b) if so, the reasons thereof; and 
(c) the steps Government propose to take in this respect, especially in 
the face of challenge posed by the neighbouring Pakistan which possesses 
atomic weapons? 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JASWANT 
SINGH): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) India is engaged in a dialogue with key interlocutors, 
including the USA and UK, on a range of issues, including the 
CTBT, on the basis of a set of voluntary proposals made by India 
after concluding the limited series of underground nuclear tests in 
May, 1998. Government's approach on the CTBT is guided solely by 
India's national interest and the building of a national consensus in 
this regard. 
While the US and UK have subscribed to positions that call for India to 
joint the NPT, our bilateral dialogues with these countries is based on the 
reality that India is a nuclear weapon State, and shall maintain a minimum 
credible nuclear deterrent in accordance with its own assessment of its 
national security requirements. 
(c) Government's decisions relating to nuclear policy will 
continue to be taken in accordance with our own assessment of 
national security requirements.

Inclusion of Arecanut, Pepper Coffee, etc. under MSP 
*372. SHRI N.K. PREMACHANDRAN: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are considering to protect the crops such as 
arecanut, pepper, coffee etc. by including the same under Minimum Support 
Price Programme; 
(b) if so, whether Government propose to announce the support price 
of the above commodities during this season; and 
(c) the reaction of Government thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE  (SHRI NITISH KUMAR): (a) 
to (c) Generally those crops are covered under Minimum Support Price 
(MSP) Scheme, which fulfil the following criteria:— 
(i) non-perishable in nature 
(ii) an item of mass consumption 
(iii) essential for food security 
(iv) basic raw material for industry 
(v) do not have widely varying cost of production 
(vi) widely grown having large area under cultivation 
Since Arecanut, Pepper and Coffee do not fulfil the above criteria, they 
are not covered under MSP and there is no proposal to cover these 
commodities under MSP. However, the interests of the growers of these 
crops are protected by taking other appropriate measures, including use of 
the instruments of trade from time to time.

However, as per literature, a disease syndrome known as Mastitis-Merit is-

Degradation of Soil and Natural Resources 
2716. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA:  
    SHRI C.M. IBRAHIM: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the grain bowl of India — Madhya Pradesh. 
Chhattisgarh, Haryana and Punjab are gradually becoming drought prone 
areas according to environmentalists; 
(b) if so, the extent of damage caused to crops this year due to drought 
conditions in these areas; 
(c) whether a high level committee has been set up tomonitor soil erosion, 
 salinity, inappropriate cropping pattern,reckless deforestation,    urban    sprawl    
 and    over-exploitation    of natural resources; and 
(d) if so, what is the latest position on the case and the action 
being taken to prevent this degradation of soil and natural resources? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHRIPAD YESSO NAIK): (a) and (b) In case of 
Haryana and Punjab no district has been categorised as drought prone. In 
case of Madhya Pradesh and Chattisgarh a total of 25 districts have been 
categorized as drought prone. During current 
62 

[14 December, 2000]        RAJYA SABHA 
year, there is drought in Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh States. In Madhya 
Pradesh, crops mainly maize, soyabean, ground nut etc. have been affected by 
drought covering 6.99 lakh ha. out of 14.56 lakh ha. sown during Kharif 
season. Similarly in Chhattisgarh State about 11.36 lakh ha. of paddy crop 
has suffered due to inadequate rainfall out of 32.44 lakh ha. sown under 
paddy. 
(c) In order to study the declining trend of agricultural 
productivity in the States of Punjab & Haryana, a Fact Finding 
Committee (FFC) was constituted under Indian Council of 
Agricultural Research, New Delhi in 1998. A Steering Committee 
was constituted in the Ministry of Agriculture to examine the 
recommendations of the FFC. With regard to sustainable agriculture, 
the following major recommendations were made for both the States. 
(i) Cultivation of summer rice should be discouraged, as it requires large 
quantities of ground water causing serious depletion in the water table. In 
place of rice, summer pulses like black gram and green gram should be 
encouraged. 
(ii) Procurement of paddy in Punjab and Haryana should be made only in 
the month of October so as to discourage early transplating of paddy 
which requires large quantity of water. 
(iii) The concessional rates, if any, on water and power available to farmer 
should be withdrawn for early and for summer rice cultivation. 
(iv) Subsidies available on inputs may be disallowed for cultivation 
of early summer rice, and 
(v) For cultivation of Basmati rice green manure crop should be 
encouraged. 
(d) Department of Agriculture and Cooperation is implementing 
various Centrally Sponsored Schemes, namely, (i) National 
Watershed Development Project for Rainfed Areas, (ii) Soil 
Conservation for Enhancing Productivity of Degraded lands in the 
Catchments of River Valley Projects and Flood Prone Rivers and (iii) 
Reclamation of Alkali Soil for the development of degraded lands.

Inefficient Handling and Storage of Food Production 
2748. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of 
CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Rs.50,000 crore worth of food production in 
India is wasted every year due to inefficient handling and storage; 
(b) out of this Rs.35,000 crore is lost due to lack of infrastructure and 
Rs.20,000 crore in transit; and 
(c) if so, what action Government are taking to stop this wastage? 
99 

RAJYA SABHA        [14 December, 2000] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OE CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHRIRAM-
CHAUHAN): (a) and (b) Exact quantum of foodgrain losses due to handling 
and storage during post harvest period is not known. However,.a Committee 
headed by Dr. V.G. Panse, in its report submitted in 1968, had estimated 
annual post harvest losses in the foodgrains^in various stages a* 9.33%. 
These included losses during threshing (1.68%), transportation (0.15%), 
processing (0.92%) rodents (2.50%) birds (0.85%), insects (2.55%) and 
moisture (0.68%). A survey conducted by the Directorate of Marketing and 
Inspection, Government of India, during 1973-74, had estimated post harvest 
losses in foodgrains to be about 5% out of which the storage losses were 
estimated at about 2.7%. A joint survey conducted by the Indian Agricultural 
Statistics Research Institute and the Indian Grain Storage Management and 
Research Institute during 1985-88 in Bulandshar district of UP had estimated 
to tat foodgrain losses at about 4.12% due to different factors at various post 
harvest stages. 
The losses during storage and transit of foodgrains in the organized 
sector is less than 0.5% and 1.5% respectively. 
(c) In order to reduce losses to foodgrains during the post harvest period 
at farm level, the Government of India had launched the Save Grain 
Campaign in 1969-70. The main thrust of activities of this scheme is training, 
demonstration and publicity in the field of scientific storage of foodgrains at 
farm level. Improvement of grain storage structures and popularisation of 
scientific storage structures like metal bins, pucca kothis and RCC ring bins 
and other activities are carried out by the Save Grain Campaign for the 
benefit of farmers. 
Foodgrain stocks at commercial level are stored by various agencies on 
scientific lines duirng which necessary prophylactic and curative measures are 
undertaken to reduce losses. 
The government^ has recently announced a National Storage Policy to 
promote bulk handling, strengthening the Save Grain Campaign to reduce 
farm level losses.

THE MINISTER OF LABOUR (DR. SATYANARAYAN JATIYA): 
(a) Child Labour is a complex socio-economic problem, which needs 
sustained efforts over a long period of time. Considering the nature and 
magnitude of the problem a gradual, progressive and sequential approach 
has been adopted for withdrawal of children from work and their 
rehabilitation. 
(b) Government has not organised any seminar on the subject 
mentioned. 
(c) and (e) Does not arise. 
(d) Government of India has been implementing two Schemes, for 
rehabilitation of children withdrawn from work, namely the scheme of 
National Child Labour Projects (NCLPs) and the scheme of Grants-in-aid to 
voluntary Organizations. 
Under the Child Labour (Prohibition & Regulation) Act, 1986 
employment of children below the age of 14 is prohibited in 13 occupations 
and 51 processes. Employers employing children in occupations and 
processes prohibited under the Act are liable for prosecution. 
Awareness generation amongst the public and also through the 
125 

RAJYA SABHA        [14 December, 2000] 
media is an important component of the strategy for elimination of child 
labour.

142 

[14 December, 2000]       RAJYA SABHA 
the context of a meeting of the Confederation of Indian Industry with the

India as an investment destination. It has, inter alia, been reported in the said 
news-item that bureacratic hurdles, corruption etc. are mainly responsible for 
foreign companies' reluctance to set up business in India. 
Making the administration corruption free, accountable, transparent and 
more effective has been on the agenda of the Government. Policies in this 
regard, have been formulated and are being continuously monitored and, wherever 
necessary, modified in order to make them more effective and responsive to the 
needs of a changing environment. 
The work of the Central Government in the field of combating corruption in 
public administration has been considerably stepped up during the last few years. 
The main step has been to reduce the role of state in society as in doing away 
with the licensing system. The Annual Action Plan prepared by the Ministry of 
Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions envisages three-pronged strategy 
comprising preventive vigilance, surveillance and detection, and deterrent 
punitive action. It was initially launched in 1985-86 and is being continued on 
annual basis. The Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 has been re-enacted, 
consolidated and effectively strengthened in 1988, to give it more teeth and to 
make it more comprehensive, The Government has also taken several steps in 
the recent past to make the vigilance machinery more effective. These include the 
steps for strengthening the institution of the Central Vigilance Commission 
(CVC). 
The Government has also taken measures to bring more transparency and 
accountability in its functioning. A large number of Ministries / Departments / 
Organisations with considerable public interface have already introduced 
Citizen's Charters indicating broadly the quality of service the public would be 
entitled to, within a specified time frame. Information and Facilitation or Help 
Counters have been set up by 65 Ministries / Departments / Central 
Government Organisations to provide information on procedures and 
143 

RAJYA SABHA        [14 December, 2000] 
the programmes and schemes of the conc erned organisation as well as to 
access information pertaining to the status of individual cases. 
The Government has also taken up simplification of laws, rules and 
procedures for improving efficiency of organisations. The Government had 
set up a Commission on Review of Administrative Laws in May, 1998 to 
make recommendations for repeal / amendments of laws, regulations, 
procedures, legislative processes with a view to improve service delivery and 
transparency in the functioning of the Government. The Commission 
submitted its report on 30 September, 1998. The important recommendations 
include repeal of almost 50 per cent of Central Laws (1382 out of 2500), 
documentation of administrative laws by all the Ministries / Department, 
development of a viable alternative disputes resolution machinery etc. Most 
of the Ministries / Departments have initiated action to bring about suitable 
amendments / modifications in or repeal of the Acts and Laws being 
administered by them. As regards the survey of the Indian Bureaucracy, 
bringing about improvements in administration is an on going process as 
detailed above.

Disparities between States regarding outlay 
         2795. SHRI RAMDAS AGARWAL: Will the PRIME MINISTER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Government have expressed serious concern over the 
widening disparities between States; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether there has been a huge gap between the approved outlay and 
expenditure in various States; 
(d) if so, the details thereof, State-wise; and 
(e) the corrective steps proposed to be taken by the Government in this 
regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE DEPARTMENT OF 
DISINVESTMENT, MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
PLANNING, MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
STATISTICS AND PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION AND 
MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE 
REFORMS AND PUBLIC GRIEVANCES OF THE MINISTRY      OF      
PERSONNEL,      PUBLIC      GRIEVANCES 
166 

[14 December, 2000]        RAJYA SABHA 
AND PENSIONS (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. Concern 
has been expressed at the widening disparities in the growth performance of 
individual States. The range of variation between the slowest and the fastest 
growing States in the 1980s was from 3.6% per year in Kerala to 6.6% in 
Rajasthan, a factor of less than 2. The range increased very substantially in 
the 1990s from a low of 2.7% per year for Bihar to a high of 9.6% of Gujarat 
a factor exceeding 3.5. Comparing Bihar's per capita growth rate with that of 
Gujarat in 1990s, the ratio between the lowest and the highest is as high as 
1:7. The States also vary very widely in terms of human development in terms 
of percentage of population below poverty line and literacy percentage etc. 
There are significant differentials between the rural and urban areas; between 
communities and between the genders in most States. 
(c) and (d) Yes, Sir. There has been a gap between the approved Plan 
outlay and expenditure in case of many States. A statement giving State-wise 
details of actual expenditure vis-a-vis approved plan outlay during the last three 
years in enclosed (see below) which indicates that many States have not been 
able to achieve the Plan outlay. The main reason for these States not 
achieving the Plan outlay is their inability to raise the projected level of 
States''own resources. 
(e) Planning Commission have been impressing upon the States to 
generate higher level of own resources, inter-alia, by improving the 
performance of State level enterprises, increasing tax and non tax revenue and 
also by curtailing their non plan expenditure so that sufficient funds are 
available to finance the plan.

Growth rate of poor States 
† 2799. SHRI P.K. MAHESHWARI: WiD the PRIME MINISTER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Planning Commission has disclosed this fact during mid 
term review of the Ninth Plan that poor States of country are getting poorer 
and their growth rate is less than half in the comparison of other States; 
(b) if so, the main reasons therefor and details in this regard. State-
wise; 
(c) whether Government are considering to increase their growth rate; 
and 
(d) if so, the concrete step taken by Government in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE DEPARTMENT OF DIS-
INVESTMENT, MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
PLANNING, MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
STATISTICS AND PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION AND MINISTER 
OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS 
AND PUBLIC GRIEVANCES OF THE MINISTRY OF PERSONNEL, 
PUBLIC GRIEVANCES AND PENSIONS (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) 
Yes, Sir. It is a fact that the mid-term review of the Ninth Five Year Plan reveals 
widening disparities regarding growth performance of individual States. The 
range of variations between the slowest and fastest growing States in 1980s was 
from 3.6% per year in Kerala to 6.6% in Rajasthan, a factor of less than 2. The 
range increased very substantially in the 1990s from a low of 2.7% per year for 
Bihar to a high of 9.6% for Gujarat, a factor exceeding 3.5. Comparing Bihar's per 
capita growth with that of Gujarat in 1990s the ratio between the lowest and 
highest is as high as 1:7. 
(b) Fiscal indicipline in the States has resulted in failure to release the 
counterpart funds for the Plan scheme s in time. In many cases the States 
have not been able to provide adequate funds for maintenance of assets 
which has resulted in their deterioration. A contributory factor is the 
capability of the Government machinery to formulate viable schemes and the 
delivery system to optimally utilize funds. Capacity for monitoring is also 
limited. Monitoring is confined to release of funds provided in the Budget 
without any reference to effective utilization and the quality of the output.  
Overall, good

different regions of India. The State-wise growth rates of per capita NSDP

(c) and (d) Yes, Sir. Planning Commission have been impressing upon 
the States to generate higher levels of own resources, inter alia by widening 
of tax .base with regard to services sector, recovery of arrears and 
enforcement of tax complaince, especially in case of direct taxes, strict 
control over wasteful expenditure through adoption of zero base budgeting 
system for all Plan and Non-Plan schemes, optimization of budget provisions 
through re-prioritization and convergence of schemes and programmes and 
speeding up of the process of disi nvestments in non-strategic PSEs 
investment, in order that adequate resources are available for strengtheing 
infrastructure, human development and other growth inducing productive 
activities.

SHOURIE); (a) The National Statistical Commission has so far held four 
meetings of the Commission as a whole from the date of its inception. The 
Commission in its first meeting held on 9th February, 2000 constituted seven 
Sub-groups for making indepth study in respect of specific subject areas to 
identify gaps and to bring up draft recommendations to the full Commission. 
These sub-groups have been meeting independently and the total number of 
sub-group meetings held so far is 33. 
The Government has not received any broad policy recommendations 
from the Commission, so far. The Commission would submit an interim 
report by the end of January 2001. 
(c) and (d) The Commission has sought extension of time upto July 
2001 for the submission of its final report. The extension of time has been 
sought in view of the fact that the Commission has to
